sense: the first of two (the former … the latter)

evidence: Sall. Cat. 54.2: ille mānsuētūdine et misericordiā clārus factus, huic sevēritās dignitātem addiderat
terms.comment: Hic, “this one”, points to the nearer of two, so usually the latter; ille, “that one”, to the farther, the former. But Latin goes by thought, not by word order: hic can be the one that matters more to the speaker, even if it was named first (Cic. Lael. 10; Lewis & Short, s.v. ille).

terms.gloss: the former, the first of two (in time or order)
evidence: Cic. Ac. 2.44: ita priōrī posterius, posteriōrī superius nōn jungitur (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fam. 1.9.24: priōre aestāte, the summer before (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Cicero sets prior against posterior, and says superior for “former” in relation to the present (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Caesar beneficiīs ac mūnificentiā magnus habēbātur, integritāte vītae Catō. ille mānsuētūdine et misericordiā clārus factus, huic sevēritās dignitātem addiderat
phrases.english: Caesar was thought great for his kindnesses and his generosity, Cato for the integrity of his life. The former had won fame by his gentleness and mercy; the latter’s strictness had added to his standing
the former was praised for his easy kindness, the latter for his firmness
